hints: Look at the start and end molecules and track the functional groups, you are going from a carboxylic acid to an alkene with the same three carbons.
Think about which hydride reagent is strong enough to reduce a carboxylic acid to a primary alcohol, $\text{LiAlH}_4$ can but $\text{NaBH}_4$ cannot.
Consider how a primary alcohol like propan-1-ol becomes propene, it needs acid-catalysed dehydration rather than a reagent used for haloalkanes.
walkthrough:
**Map the overall change**

Think of this as a friendly two-step journey. You start with propanoic acid and finish with propene.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOH} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH=CH}_2$$
The sensible middle stop is propan-1-ol, so step 1 is reduction and step 2 is dehydration.

**Choose the reducing agent for stage 1**

Carboxylic acids are quite resistant to reduction. You need a very strong reducing agent.

$\text{LiAlH}_4$ reduces carboxylic acids to primary alcohols, but $\text{NaBH}_4$ is too mild and only reduces aldehydes and ketones. So the first stage must be $\text{LiAlH}_4$:
$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOH} \xrightarrow{\text{LiAlH}_4} \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$$

**Choose the reagent for stage 2**

Now you need to remove water from an alcohol to form a C=C double bond. This is dehydration.

Concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ with heat does this perfectly. $\text{NaOH}$ in ethanol is for eliminating $\text{HX}$ from a haloalkane, not for dehydrating an alcohol:
$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH} \xrightarrow{\text{conc. H}_2\text{SO}_4} \text{CH}_3\text{CH=CH}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$
That combination matches $\text{LiAlH}_4$ then conc. $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$.

options.A: Correct. $\text{LiAlH}_4$ reduces propanoic acid to propan-1-ol, then conc. $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ dehydrates propan-1-ol to propene. Both reagents fit their functional group transformations.
options.B: Incorrect. The first stage is right, $\text{LiAlH}_4$ does give propan-1-ol. But $\text{NaOH}$ in ethanol is used for dehydrohalogenation of a bromoalkane or chloroalkane, it will not dehydrate an alcohol to an alkene.
options.C: Incorrect. The second stage reagent is right for an alcohol, but the first stage fails. $\text{NaBH}_4$ is too weak to reduce a carboxylic acid, so no propan-1-ol would form and the synthesis stops at step 1.
options.D: Incorrect. Neither step works here. $\text{NaBH}_4$ cannot reduce propanoic acid, and $\text{NaOH}$ in ethanol cannot dehydrate an alcohol. This pair confuses reduction strength and elimination conditions.
